Five strips, ten wavelengths, one dimension

The split is a result, not a labelling convention. Short wavelengths move 0.53–0.59 in log₁₀ reflectance per decade of concentration; everything from amber rightwards moves 0.02–0.09 and is therefore a brightness reference, not a concentration channel.

BRIEFWhat was asked

Reproduced verbatim, with the two amendments that arrived while the work was running.

Original request

Beginning of analysis.
I have 5 test images in captures.  X15.h5, C1002.h5, C1003.h5, C1004.h5, C1005.h5
Supposedly at 10, 256, 128, 64, 64 ppb.
Read some of the image files.
The white correction should be using the same gray patches that we fit before.
We need to do a couple of things for the analysis:
1) sample area confirmation.  The sample roi is approximate.  Figure out an edge detection method and adjust the rect.
2) analysis. I had thought to simple come in from the edge a bit and measure the color average over the smaller rect.
   But I observe that that there is an edge color effect that is sometimes large and pronounced.
   I don't have enough images yet to sort out whether that effect is really meaningful and interpretable, but I think we may need to consider it.  In that case we could revert to ANN, or to characterizing the color distributions and using some distribution parameters in addition to the mean in the analysis.
3) The original concept is to read a bunch of training images with known ppb, compute their color magnitudes  per LED + bayer channel, run a PCA to identify the important channels, perform PCA on the magnitudes (and now maybe on other measures), and somehow end up with a mapping to the ppb concentration.

For now, I want you to give a try at working through these images, try a few things, and let me know what seems to work or not work.

Amendment — constraint

I don't want you to edit any source code. There is another agent looking at it.

Amendment — sample provenance

Carry on. sample X15 is actually expired, but is visually unchanged.  It's the only sample available at the moment and is a true 10 ppb representative.

Amendment — the pad's geometry

The edge finding algorithm has captured significant area outside of the true paper pad, particularly on the right hand side.  There is some non-black material surrounding the pad.  The algorithm can use this additional information:
1) the chemical pad shape is rectangular
2) the chemical pad will not be rotated more than about 1 degree off of the camera orientation.
3) The chemical pad will always be the same height and width, only the origin will shift, and very slightly the rotation.
4) The left and right edges of the chemical pad will be aligned with the left and right edges of the white un-died part of the strip that is visible below the pad.  This may affect your interpretations.

That last amendment arrived after the first pass and is the reason for revision 2. Every number below is from the corrected segmentation; where a conclusion moved, both figures are given.

Nothing in src/, devdesk/ or the database was written to. The analysis ran out of a scratch directory against read-only copies, and the published layermodels rows were read but never superseded.

TL;DRWhat came out

Four numbers that between them decide what to do next.

0.21%
Median spread of reflectance across the three exposure rungs. The dark subtraction and white correction are sound.
0.2%
Agreement between the two 64 ppb strips in photo_red — the instrument's photometric and placement floor.
13–25%
Disagreement between those same two strips in the dye-sensitive channels. Purely chromatic, so it is real chemistry.
1.18%
Spread of X15 ÷ C1005 across all 27 cells. The 10 ppb strip and a 64 ppb strip are the same colour.
Works

Locating the pad from the white paper below it rather than from its own colour; white correction re-anchored on the region actually measured; exposure invariance as the check that both are right.

Doesn't

Thresholding the pad against its surroundings — the channel it sits in is not black and not blue. PCA finding several useful channels — there is only one dimension to find. Separating 10 ppb from 64 ppb by any optical means, on this evidence.

1Finding the sample area

The seeded ROI is not merely approximate — it is about half the pad's area, and the pad moves underneath it.

First attempt, and the trap it fell into

The obvious method is a threshold on blue-over-green. The pad reads B/G 0.25–0.27 against 0.47 for white paper: wide separation in all five captures, and illumination-independent, so it needs no correction first. Grow the strip with Otsu on total intensity, threshold B/G inside it, take the largest component. It found a pad every time.

It also found up to 16% more than the pad, and always on one side.

The reason is that the strip does not sit against black. It lies in a channel whose floor is a dull olive material, and that floor reads B/G ≈ 0.33 — less blue than the paper, only a little bluer than the pad. Any threshold placed between paper and pad swallows it. How much it swallows depends on which wall the strip was pushed against: the strip's x-position varies by 9 layer px across these five captures, so between 2 and 12 px of channel floor shows on each side, and the excess lands on the right in X15 and C1002 and on the left in the other three.

This is the failure mode a threshold cannot be tuned out of. The floor sits between the two classes being separated, so any cut that keeps all of the pad keeps some of the floor as well.

The method that works

The fix is to stop asking the pad's own colour where its sides are. Four properties of the hardware make that possible:

  • the pad is a rectangle;
  • it is rotated no more than about a degree from the sensor axes;
  • its width and height are fixed — only the origin moves;
  • its left and right edges are the left and right edges of the white undyed paper visible below it.

The last one is what makes it work. The paper below the pad is the one surface inside the channel that is unambiguous — it is the only thing there that is both bright and blue. Locating it locates the pad's two long edges, without the pad's colour entering into it anywhere.

  1. Paperness = B/G × clip(tot ÷ ½·paper_level, 0, 1). B/G alone separates paper from channel floor and ignores shading, but the thin dark gap between paper and channel reads as a high-B/G line and would extend the run. The brightness factor pushes that line back down without moving either plateau.
  2. Long edges: per-row subpixel crossings of paperness through the paper band below the pad, fitted as two parallel lines with one shared slope. Fitting the two edges independently over a 30-row band leaves ±2° of tilt uncertainty, which swamps the real tilt; the rigid-strip constraint drops the residual to 0.05–0.28 px.
  3. Ends: the long run of low B/G down the strip's interior columns, with subpixel crossings at each end. This is the only place the pad's own colour is used, and only along the strip axis, where nothing but paper borders it.
  4. Rectangle: transform to strip coordinates u across and v down. Depth is then the exact distance to the rectangle boundary — the smallest of four edge distances — rather than a distance transform of a ragged blob.

How the four priors held up

Rectangle

The edge residual is 0.05–0.28 layer px over 29–34 rows. The strip's sides are straight to well under a pixel; nothing about the data argues against a rectangle.

Rotation

Four of five are within ±0.72°. C1005 sits at −2.09°, outside the ±1° the fixture is expected to hold — confirmed independently by three different row bands and by both edges separately. The fit is therefore left unconstrained in angle. A hard ±1° clamp would have mis-seated that strip by about 0.9 px at the pad's corners.

Fixed size

Height holds outright: 52.96 ± 0.30 px across all five, a spread of 0.6%.

Width holds where the strip stands clear of the channel walls. The three strips with ≥3.7 px of floor showing on both sides measure 41.11 ± 0.21 px. The two pushed hard against the left wall — X15 and C1002, whose left edges agree with each other to 0.16 px and are the leftmost of the set — measure 39.89 and 38.54. The wall's lip is hiding 1.2 and 2.6 px of paper. That is a measurement artefact, not narrower strips, and it is exactly what prior 3 is for: fixed_size=True snaps the rectangle to the pooled width about the measured centre.

Paper = pad

On C1003, the strip with the weakest rim of the five, the pad's own left and right edges sit 0.13 px and −0.56 px from the paper's. On the others the pad's rim makes its own edges unmeasurable — the reflectance is still falling where the edge should be — which is precisely why anchoring on the paper is the right move rather than a convenience.

Every reflectance rises, because the material removed was darker than the pad: median +3.4%, worst +7.1%. The pad is still roughly double the seeded 34 × 34 box, and its centre still wanders ±3 layer px between placements, so the case for segmenting at all is unchanged — moving from the seeded box to the found pad changes the answer by up to 14% in C1005.

Bearing

No conclusion in sections 2 and 3 reverses. Three sharpen: the photometric rim turns out to be uniform across all five strips rather than varying by seating; the instrument's replicate floor improves from ~1% to 0.2%; and X15 and C1005 become more alike, not less. The corrected mask makes the chemistry-limited conclusion stronger, because the geometric term it competes against is now smaller and better measured.

Carrying the white correction across

Because the measured region moves, the published w1/w2 — which answer "what is the illumination at roi 32" — are the wrong weights for it. Each cell's fitted surface was rebuilt from its stored coef_json and re-anchored on the region actually measured, by the same formula the calibration used:

g1, gs, g2 = mean gain over chip1 / region / chip2
t  = fractional x-position of the region between the chips
w1 = (1 − t)·gs/g1   w2 = t·gs/g2
divisor = w1·mean(chip1) + w2·mean(chip2)

Put the region back at roi 32 and this reproduces the published weights to 0.0000% on all 27 usable cells — once anchor_form is honoured, since photo_red.Gr and violet.B were published as 1anchor and take the least-squares form instead.

2The edge effect

It is two superimposed effects with different causes, different ranges, and — for one of them — no consistent sign.

The decisive test was a control the images already contained: the unstained white paper below the pad. Same strip, same height, same illumination, no chemistry. Profile its reflectance against distance from its own edge and you learn how much of the pad's rim belongs to the strip's geometry rather than to the reagent.

This control is also where the segmentation fix mattered most. In the first pass the control region was grown from the strip component and so included channel floor, which made the paper appear to keep falling out to 8–10 px in three of the five captures. Taken from the paperness mask instead, the paper recovers within 2–4 px in all five — the photometric rim is a uniform property of the strip standing proud of the stage, not something that varies with how it was seated.

Two things are worth noticing in that table. The chemical rim reaches 10–13 px, three times the photometric one — so the two effects are separable by depth as well as by colour. And ordering the 1–2 px column by concentration gives −27.9 (10 ppb), −24.9 and −42.1 (both 64), −13.8 (128), +22.0 (256): monotone in concentration except for C1004, which is the same strip that is anomalous in every other respect. With one strip per level that is a hypothesis, not a result — but it is a cheap one to test, and if it holds the rim is information rather than contamination.

Settled

Erode 10 layer px — 20 px in stream space. That leaves 627–704 pixels, which is ample. Erode 4 now clears the photometric rim, but the chemical one runs to 10–13 px; past 10 the reference channels stop improving.

The dye channels never converge, and that is the finding rather than a failure of the erosion: what remains is a real difference between the two strips.

Ruled out

No linear projection removes the rim. In a pixel-level PCA over all 10,687 pad pixels, PC1 correlates with depth at only r = 0.55, and PC2 — the colour axis — still shifts substantially when the rim is included, because the rim's chemistry differs, not just its brightness. The rim has to be excluded geometrically.

Which channels are worth using

Correlation with ppb is the wrong figure of merit — it will happily promote a channel whose slope is smaller than the strip-to-strip spread. Fitting log₁₀R = a + b·log₁₀(ppb) on the four C-strips and dividing the slope by the fit residual gives something usable:

photo_red scores a respectable S/N on a slope twenty-two times smaller than cyan's, purely because its residuals are eighteen times smaller too. That makes it an excellent control — it is measuring geometry and photometry almost alone — and a fragile concentration channel, since its whole range across a 4× concentration span is about 4%. violet.B is the weakest, and along with royal_blue.B carries the largest off-axis residuals, which is consistent with the card-fluorescence behaviour already on record for the short wavelengths.

The two things standing in the way

Chemistry

The two 64 ppb strips differ by 13–25% in the dye channels while agreeing to 0.2% in photo_red. A difference that is purely chromatic cannot be placement, exposure, or illumination — those move every channel together. The two strips really do carry different dye loads.

Instrument ≈ 0.2%. Chemistry ≈ 25%. The optics are not the limiting factor and improving them will not help.

X15

A rank-1 model — one fixed spectral shape times a per-strip dye loading — captures 98.53% of the between-strip variance. So a strip's colour tells you its loading and essentially nothing else.

X15 ÷ C1005 across all 27 cells has mean 0.989 and a spread of 1.18%: flat, at the level of measurement noise, and flatter than before the segmentation was corrected. For contrast, X15 ÷ C1004 has a spread of 9.65%, because those two strips genuinely differ. Taking X15 at face value as 10 ppb, no choice of LEDs, no PCA and no ANN can separate it from a 64 ppb strip, because there is no spectral feature to separate them on.

The distribution parameters were worth trying and did not rescue it. Within-pad CV, p90 − p10 and skew of the colour index do not flag C1004 as the odd strip — its CV is in fact the lowest of the five at 4.53%, because its bullseye is a smooth low-amplitude gradient rather than a noisy one.

NEXTCaveats, and what to capture

Five captures, four levels, one replicate pair. Everything above is indicative.

  • The pad's sides now come from the white paper and are independent of the chemistry, but its ends are still found from the B/G step down the strip. A 0 ppb blank will not give that step and will need the ends fixed by geometry — the offset from the strip's tip, which these five captures agree on to within a few px. The sides and the tilt would survive unchanged.
  • The pooled width and height come from five captures of one strip lot. Re-derive them for a different lot before relying on fixed_size.
  • One strip of five sits at −2.09°, outside the ±1° the fixture is expected to hold. Worth knowing whether that is the strip, the channel, or how it was loaded.
  • X15 is expired. Everything here treats it as a true 10 ppb representative as instructed, which is what makes its position a finding rather than a labelling error — but a single expired strip cannot establish that the assay fails to resolve 10 from 64 ppb.
  • Two of 27 cells were published under 1anchor. Any code that recomputes weights must read anchor_form rather than assume the majority form.

The most valuable next captures, in order:

  1. Replicates at each level, n ≥ 3. Without them the assay's own variance cannot be separated from the level, and that variance is currently the dominant term.
  2. A fresh 10 ppb strip. This decides whether the low-end problem belongs to the expiry or to the assay.
  3. A blank. Both to anchor the calibration and to force the end-detection fallback to be built.
  4. Two strips of the same level seated at opposite ends of the channel. Cheap, and it settles whether the width difference between wall-jammed and clear strips is really the wall's lip.
